extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media industry observers
extracted.subtask_description: A commentary-style daily media newsletter item assessing recent newsroom errors, corrections, sourcing practices, and broader implications for journalistic standards and opinion-page labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly issue clear corrections when errors occur
rubrics_metrics.description: News outlets should take responsibility and issue corrections when reporting is inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: The Post removed assertions that OAN and Giuliani received FBI warnings; The Times corrected misstating whether Giuliani received a formal F.B.I. warning; NBC News published an online correction and changed the premise and headline of the article to reflect corrected information. Corrections should identify the earlier error and state what was changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify anonymous sources thoroughly before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about stories that are partly based on anonymous sources; major claims should not rest solely on such sourcing without strong verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes all three outlets 'partly based their stories on anonymous sources' and treats that as a troubling factor. Implicit anti-pattern: relying on one anonymous source to assert high-impact facts (e.g., that someone received a defensive briefing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between prepared and delivered official actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm whether an action (such as an FBI defensive briefing) was actually delivered versus merely prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NBC's correction explained a second source said the briefing was 'only prepared for Giuliani and not delivered to him.' Reporters should verify this distinction before asserting someone 'received' a formal warning or briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect source confidentiality while balancing accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms generally will not reveal sources who provided information, even when the veracity of that information is questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giuliani demanded that 'the Post and Times “must reveal their sources who lied,”' but the piece notes 'Of course, the Post and Times are not going to reveal those sources.' Guidance: protect confidential sources as a standard practice unless extraordinary reasons dictate otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct internal high-level editorial reviews after significant errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious conversations should take place inside newsrooms among high-level editors to examine sourcing and editorial choices after problematic reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states you'd 'like to think there are (or have been) serious conversations going on inside the newsrooms of the Post and Times with high-level editors to talk about those sources and how this all went down.' This implies a rubric of post-mortem review and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: If foundational facts change, update headline and premise
rubrics_metrics.description: When corrected information undermines the original premise, outlets should change the headline and the framing of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NBC changed 'the premise and headline of the article below' after learning the briefing was prepared but not delivered. This is an editorial best practice to avoid misleading readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the basis of corrections, including contradictory sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should state why the original report was wrong (e.g., new or contradictory source information) and be transparent about the sources of the correction when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NBC's correction explained the report 'was based on a source familiar with the matter, but a second source now says...' — showing that corrections should note when additional reporting changes the factual picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuous commitment to accuracy to protect reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate and reputable news outlets should be 'constantly striving to get it right' and be as upset about errors as their audiences; this sustained effort underpins credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues the Post, Times and NBC are 'constantly striving to get it right' and that taking responsibility for mistakes is important because 'it's their reputations that will take a hit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of partisan perceptions and the impact of errors on trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should recognize the political climate and how errors may reinforce distrust among partisan audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes this is 'a troubling look' in a climate where conservatives 'believe the media has it out for them,' implying reporters should consider how coverage and mistakes will be perceived and potentially weaponized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify the role and labeling of opinion content
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion sections should make clear their purpose (to argue how the world can/should be) and adjust labeling to match intent (e.g., changing 'op-eds' to 'guest essays').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kathleen Kingsbury is quoted: 'What we are trying to do every day — our news pages are showing the world as it is. Our opinion pages are really trying to tell our readers how the world can and, perhaps, should be.' The Times renamed 'op-eds' to 'guest essays,' a change described as 'long overdue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in training, fact-checking, and professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and promote journalism training, fact-checking events, and seminars to improve reporting standards and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists resources and events (Covering COVID-19 with Al Tompkins, Professor’s Press Pass, United Facts of America, Summit for Reporters and Editors) and highlights newsroom leadership programs, implying ongoing education is part of maintaining quality journalism.
